name: Body recomposition / calorie deficit

card.summary: Eating below maintenance to lose body fat, including from the face, usually paired with protein and lifting; fat loss cannot be targeted to the face.
card.aka: Cutting, leaning out, fat loss diet
card.note: Aggressive deficits carry documented risks; looksmaxxing forum users debate deficits during puberty.

quick.overview:
A calorie deficit means eating less energy than the body uses, so stored fat is drawn on. In looksmaxxing it is the common answer to facial fat: people say lowering overall body fat reveals the jaw and cheekbones. Body recomposition refers to losing fat while keeping or building muscle.

Reference sources describe energy balance as the basis of fat loss. Forum discussion focuses on how large a deficit to run, body-fat targets, and whether cutting during puberty affects growth.
quick.mechanism: When intake is below expenditure, hormonal changes favor releasing fatty acids from fat stores. Reference material recommends adequate protein and resistance training to help retain lean mass during a deficit, and notes the body adapts, so weight loss often falls short of simple arithmetic.
quick.risks: Reference sources list fatigue, irritability, hair loss and menstrual irregularities in the short term, and nutrient deficiency, muscle loss, bone density loss and gallstones with very large deficits. Adolescents are named as a group vulnerable to progression from restrictive dieting to an eating disorder.

lead: A calorie deficit occurs when energy intake is lower than total daily energy expenditure, so the body supplies the shortfall mainly from stored fat [1]. Body recomposition is the related goal of reducing fat while maintaining or increasing lean mass, typically discussed alongside resistance training and higher protein intake [1].

In looksmaxxing communities it is the standard approach to facial fat: proponents say that reducing overall body fat is how the jawline and cheekbones become more visible, and forum threads debate target body-fat percentages, deficit size and timing [2]. A reference summary describes a sustainable deficit and warns that large deficits carry risks [1].
infobox: Higher protein intake and resistance training [1]
Not directed to a chosen area; determined by the individual (see Claims)

paras: Total daily energy expenditure combines basal metabolic rate, physical activity and the energy cost of digestion. When intake is below this total, the difference is made up largely from fat stores. Reference material gives a deficit of roughly 500 to 1,000 kcal per day, or about 0.5 to 1 kg per week, as a sustainable range, though the same source also gives smaller figures in places [1].

Lower insulin and raised glucagon and epinephrine trigger release of fatty acids from fat tissue [1]. The older rule that about 3,500 kcal equals a pound of fat is described as a rough guide that often overestimates loss because of metabolic adaptation and water shifts, and a 2018 trial is cited as showing individual differences in fat versus lean loss [1].

The reference summary recommends 1.6 to 2.2 g of protein per kg per day and resistance training three to four times weekly to support lean mass during a deficit. It cites a 2016 trial of athletes eating about 40% below maintenance in which a higher-protein group with resistance training gained lean mass and lost fat over four weeks [1].

Short-term effects named include fatigue, irritability, hair loss and menstrual irregularities. Deficits above 1,000 kcal per day, or very low intakes without supervision, are linked to nutrient deficiencies, muscle loss and metabolic slowdown, while diets of about 800 kcal per day or less are linked to gallstones. Bone density loss and eating disorders are also listed [1]. A 2016 study of contestants from a televised weight-loss show found resting metabolic rate still far below predictions six years later [1]. Deficits are described as contraindicated in pregnancy and type 1 diabetes [1].

Forum threads ask how much to cut, with users in one thread advising a 17-year-old to reach about 15% body fat and hold there rather than cut aggressively, and others advising against cutting during puberty [2]. Reference material gives little age-specific guidance beyond naming adolescents as vulnerable to eating disorders [1].

Trials of calorie-restricted diets exist in obesity research, such as a 48-week randomized trial of 90 obese adults on dairy- and fiber-enriched energy-reduced diets with a 500 kcal per day deficit [3]. No studies found specifically of calorie deficits for facial appearance.

lore.intro: Forum users discuss cutting as the way to reveal facial structure and argue over deficit size and the effect of dieting in puberty [2].

claims.claim: Losing body fat reveals the jaw and cheekbones.
claims.believers: Users say a lean face looks sharper and recommend reaching around 15% body fat [2].
claims.experts: Reference material describes fat loss through a calorie deficit but does not address facial appearance specifically [1].

claims.claim: Teens in puberty should not cut calories.
claims.believers: Forum replies advise maintaining or gaining during puberty and cutting later, and some warn a deficit will stunt growth [2].
claims.experts: Reference material gives little age-specific guidance but names adolescents as vulnerable to restrictive dieting progressing to eating disorders [1].

claims.claim: Higher protein with lifting preserves muscle in a cut.
claims.believers: Posters recommend lifting while cutting to stay lean without losing muscle [2].
claims.experts: A reference summary cites guidance of 1.6 to 2.2 g/kg protein and resistance training, and a 2016 athlete trial reporting fat loss with lean mass gain [1].
